title: DeepMind reinforcement-learning controller shapes TCV plasmas, including sustained twin “droplets”
summary: DeepMind's deep reinforcement learning controller, commanding all 19 TCV coils, produced and held elongated, negative-triangularity, snowflake and twin-droplet plasmas at EPFL's Swiss Plasma Center.
account: Degrave et al. (Nature, received 14 July 2021, published 16 February 2022) describe a single deep neural network controller. It learns in simulation to command all 19 magnetic control coils of the Tokamak à Configuration Variable (TCV). TCV is a research tokamak at the Swiss Plasma Center, EPFL. Deployed on the real device, the controller produced and controlled elongated conventional shapes and advanced configurations such as negative triangularity and “snowflake” plasmas. It tracked location, current and shape. In one demonstration it established a snowflake with X-points 34 cm apart and narrowed the separation to 6.6 cm with a combined root-mean-square error of 3.7 cm. It also sustained “droplets”, two separate plasmas maintained simultaneously in the vessel. The experiment dates are not given. MIT Technology Review (16 February 2022) reported that the AI controlled the real reactor without additional fine-tuning. It quoted independent expert Jonathan Citrin of the Dutch Institute for Fundamental Energy Research and Swiss Plasma Center director Ambrogio Fasoli. In a preprint of 21 July 2023, DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center reported upgraded controllers with up to 65% better shape accuracy in simulation and new validating experiments on TCV. This follow-up appeared in Fusion Engineering and Design in March 2024. On 21 January 2026, a team from Next Step Fusion and U.S. institutions, with no DeepMind or EPFL authors, reported that deep reinforcement learning controllers kept errors in plasma shape within 1.5 to 2.0 cm on the DIII-D tokamak.
purpose: The controller was built to shape and maintain plasmas in TCV from high-level objectives; the configurations produced, including droplets, were its intended use.
system: DeepMind deep reinforcement learning magnetic controller for TCV (MLP policy commanding 19 coils)
developer: DeepMind, with the Swiss Plasma Center, EPFL
taxonomy_note: The result is a control capability on a research tokamak rather than an accuracy gain over a baseline.

ratings.reason: The Swiss Plasma Center gained a controller that the authors call a notable advance for tokamak feedback control. The controller reduced the design effort for new configurations and made new droplet experiments possible.
No societal outcome beyond research progress is documented.

ai_role.statement: The reinforcement learning policy directly issued the coil voltage commands during the discharges, so the configurations are its output. The evidence is the peer-reviewed paper by the maker (DeepMind) and the operator (EPFL) plus an independent news report quoting an outside expert. Developer and deployer collaborated on the paper.

In a preprint of 21 July 2023, DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center reported upgraded controllers with up to 65% better shape accuracy in simulation and new validating experiments on TCV. On 21 January 2026, a team from Next Step Fusion and U.S. institutions, with no DeepMind or EPFL authors, reported that deep reinforcement learning controllers kept errors in plasma shape within 1.5 to 2.0 cm on the DIII-D tokamak.

fields.account: Degrave et al. (Nature, received 14 July 2021, published 16 February 2022) describe a single deep neural network controller. It learns in simulation to command all 19 magnetic control coils of the Tokamak à Configuration Variable (TCV). TCV is a research tokamak at the Swiss Plasma Center, EPFL. Deployed on the real device, the controller produced and controlled elongated conventional shapes and advanced configurations such as negative triangularity and “snowflake” plasmas. It tracked location, current and shape. In one demonstration it established a snowflake with X-points 34 cm apart and narrowed the separation to 6.6 cm with a combined root-mean-square error of 3.7 cm. It also sustained “droplets”, two separate plasmas maintained simultaneously in the vessel. The experiment dates are not given. MIT Technology Review (16 February 2022) reported that the AI controlled the real reactor without additional fine-tuning. It quoted independent expert Jonathan Citrin of the Dutch Institute for Fundamental Energy Research and Swiss Plasma Center director Ambrogio Fasoli. In a preprint of 21 July 2023, DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center reported upgraded controllers with up to 65% better shape accuracy in simulation and new validating experiments on TCV. This follow-up appeared in Fusion Engineering and Design in March 2024. On 21 January 2026, a team from Next Step Fusion and U.S. institutions, with no DeepMind or EPFL authors, reported that deep reinforcement learning controllers kept errors in plasma shape within 1.5 to 2.0 cm on the DIII-D tokamak.
